Stability of learned node importance in citation networks

Results report - Capstone Project Phase B (26-2-R-2). Niran Czuckermann and Shahar Bar. Advisor: Dr. Dvora Toledano-Kitai. Braude College of Engineering. 21 November 2026.

How this report is organised. Part I is the study planned in Phase A, on the PubMed-Diabetes citation network. Part II checks how far its conclusions go: the same experiment on two more citation networks (Cora and CiteSeer) and a version of the forest without the closeness feature.

Main findings - Part I (PubMed-Diabetes)
  • The primary forest keeps the top 10 % of the ranking more stable than PageRank, the measure it learns, in 6 of 9 settings, mainly when citations are added; over all papers it is as stable as PageRank on average.
  • It is never more stable than the best simple measure (degree, k-core or closeness).
  • The Phase A design, with PageRank as input and target, gives a forest that copies PageRank; that is why the primary forest has no PageRank input.
Part II (more datasets, no closeness)
  • On Cora and CiteSeer the forest is not more stable than PageRank: it keeps the top 10 % more stable in none of the 9 settings in either dataset, so the PubMed-Diabetes result does not carry over.
  • Without closeness the forest predicts PageRank much worse in all three datasets and is less stable in two of them: keep closeness.

Part I - The main study: PubMed-Diabetes

1. The method in one page

Research question (Phase A). Does a Random Forest that combines several centrality measures give node rankings that are more stable under edge noise than any single measure? A ranking is stable if the same papers stay on top when the citation data is incomplete or partly wrong.

The steps in Figure 1, in plain words:

  1. Clean the graph. Every paper is a node, every citation a directed edge (A cites B: A to B). Duplicates, self-citations, unknown papers and citation loops are removed, because a paper can only cite older papers.
  2. Compute five centralities for every paper (Table 1).
  3. Scale them to [0, 1] with a Min-Max scaler that is fitted once, on the original graph, and never again (the "frozen scaler" of Phase A). On a damaged graph a scaled value may fall outside [0, 1]; it is not clipped.
  4. Train the Random Forest on the original graph. Its target is the PageRank of each paper. Two versions are trained: without PageRank among its inputs (the primary model) and with it (the control, see Section 3).
  5. Base scores and ranking. The two forests and the five single centralities each give every paper a score; scores become ranks (1 = most important, equal scores share the mean rank).
  6. Damage the graph in three ways and three sizes (Table 2); repeat 30 times each, which gives 270 damaged graphs.
  7. Re-score every damaged graph: recompute the features, apply the same frozen scaler, apply the same forests (no retraining), and rank again.
  8. Measure how far each new ranking is from the base ranking (Table 3). The method whose ranking moves least is the most stable.
Table 1. The five features (one number per paper).
FeatureWhat it measuresHow it is computed here
Degreedirect citation links(citations given + received) / (N - 1)
Betweennesshow often the paper lies on a shortest path between two othersexact, directed, divided by (N - 1)(N - 2)
Closenesshow quickly the rest of the network reaches the paper through citationsincoming distances with the Wasserman-Faust correction (decision D17)
PageRanka paper is important if important papers cite itdamping 0.85
k-corehow deep the paper sits in a densely connected groupon the undirected graph, without self-loops
Table 2. The three kinds of damage. Each is applied to 5 %, 10 % and 20 % of the citations.
KindWhat happensWhat it imitates
Remove citationsrandom citations are deletedmissing data
Add random citationsrandom citations between any two papers are addedwrong citations (may create impossible loops)
Add citations newer to olderrandom citations are added, but only from a newer to an older paperwrong citations that are still possible in time
Table 3. How the new ranking is compared with the base ranking (every method against its own base ranking).
MeasureQuestion it answersBest value
Spearman (all papers)is the whole order the same? 1 = identical, 0 = unrelated1
Top-10 % stayin what share of the damaged graphs does a top-10 % paper stay in the top 10 %?1
Instability (CV)how much does one paper's score jump across the 30 damaged graphs?0

Spearman over all papers can be flattering for methods with many ties (k-core has about 10 different values), so the top-10 % measure is used next to it: it only looks at the papers that matter. The forests are trained to imitate PageRank, so PageRank is their natural comparison; degree and k-core measure a different kind of importance.

2. The dataset and its cleaning

PubMed-Diabetes (Namata et al., 2012): 19,717 papers from PubMed about diabetes, in three classes and 44,338 directed citations. Cleaning removed 14 citations (0.03 %): 11 citations that closed a loop, 3 self-citations (loops: the higher PubMed id is kept as the newer paper); no paper was removed. Result: 19,717 papers and 44,324 citations, no loops, one connected network.

As Figure 2 shows, 10 % of the papers are never cited and 80 % cite no other paper of the dataset (it only keeps citations between its own papers), while the most cited paper has 171 citations. Most papers therefore sit at the end of a citation chain; this is why betweenness is 0 for most papers and why closeness needed a careful definition.

3. Why there are two Random Forests: with and without PageRank

What Phase A said. The feature vector of a paper holds five numbers, including PageRank (Phase A, Model Definition: Node Representation), and the forest is trained to predict PageRank (Phase A, Model Definition: Target Variable, and Appendix A). PageRank is therefore both an input and the answer.

Why that does not work. A forest that is given the answer as an input learns to copy it. The result is PageRank with a little noise, so comparing its stability with PageRank's says nothing about combining several measures. In PubMed-Diabetes the forest with PageRank puts 99.8 % of its weight on that one input (Figure 3).

What we do. We train both. The control forest is Phase A exactly as written. The primary forest is the same forest with PageRank removed from its inputs, so it has to rebuild importance from degree, betweenness, closeness and k-core. The conclusions are drawn from the primary forest; the control shows what the original design does.

Table 4. How well each forest predicts PageRank on papers it was not trained on (80 % train, 20 % test), PubMed-Diabetes.
ForestR²SpearmanLargest input weight
With PageRank (control)1.001.00PageRank 99.8 %
Without PageRank (primary)0.750.80closeness 47 %, degree 44 %
Best single centrality alone-0.73closeness

Which is better, and why. The primary forest predicts PageRank worse (Table 4), as it must, because it is not given the answer; it still follows PageRank better than any single centrality. It is the better test of the research question, because its stability is free to differ from PageRank's. The control cannot do better than PageRank: its Spearman is 0.06 lower on average and up to 0.14 lower after damage, because a tree cannot predict outside the range it was trained on, and many scaled values leave that range once citations are added.

4. Experiment results

Every method is compared with its own base ranking after each of the 270 damaged graphs. Figure 4 shows the whole order (Spearman) and Figure 5 whether the most important 10 % of the papers stay on top. Methods with many tied scores (k-core, degree) reach 1.0 in the second measure partly because tied papers do not change places.

Against PageRank (Figure 6). The primary forest keeps the top 10 % more stable than PageRank in 6 of 9 settings (on average +0.15), mainly when citations are added, while the order over all papers is the same on average (+0.000): better when citations are added, worse when they are removed.

Against the single measures (Table 5). In none of the 9 settings is the primary forest more stable than the best of degree, k-core, closeness and betweenness.

Table 5. PubMed-Diabetes at the strongest damage (20 % of the citations).

5. Answers to the hypotheses (PubMed-Diabetes)

Table 6. The three Phase A hypotheses on PubMed-Diabetes (primary forest, averages over the 9 damage settings).
HypothesisVerdictEvidence
H1: a combined score is more stable than single measuresPartlymore stable than PageRank at the top in 6 of 9 settings; never more stable than the best single measure
H2: the forest copes with the failure of one feature by using the othersNot supportedthe control relies 99.8 % on PageRank and is less stable than PageRank; the primary forest relies 47 % on closeness
H3: the network core keeps its high rankSupported (adjusted core rule)core papers stay in the top 10 % in 81 % of the damaged graphs, other important papers in 63 %; Phase A's own core rule gives an empty core (decision D16)

Table 6 sums up Part I: combining centralities makes the top of the ranking more robust than PageRank against added citations, but not against missing ones, and simple local measures remain the most stable.

Part II - How far do the results go?

The lecturer asked two questions about Part I: would the results be the same on other citation networks, and does the forest do better without closeness? Part II answers both with the same code, the same damage and the same 30 repeats.

6. Two more citation networks

  • PubMed-Diabetes (Namata et al., 2012): 19,717 papers from PubMed about diabetes, in three classes and 44,338 directed citations. Cleaning removed 14 citations (0.03 %): 11 citations that closed a loop, 3 self-citations (loops: the higher PubMed id is kept as the newer paper); no paper was removed. Result: 19,717 papers and 44,324 citations, no loops, one connected network.
  • Cora (McCallum et al., 2000; LINQS version, Sen et al., 2008): 2,708 machine-learning papers in seven classes and 5,429 directed citations. Cleaning removed 155 citations (2.9 %): 155 citations that closed a loop (loops: the fewest citations that leave no loop, since there are no dates); no paper was removed. Result: 2,708 papers and 5,274 citations, no loops, 78 separate pieces.
  • CiteSeer (Giles et al., 1998; LINQS version, Sen et al., 2008): 3,312 computer-science papers in six classes and 4,732 directed citations. Cleaning removed 197 citations (4.2 %): 124 self-citations, 56 citations that closed a loop, 17 citations to papers missing from the dataset (loops: the fewest citations that leave no loop, since there are no dates), and then 48 papers left without any citation (1.4 %). Result: 3,264 papers and 4,535 citations, no loops, 390 separate pieces.

All three are cleaned with the same steps in the same order; only the rule for citation loops differs, because Cora and CiteSeer have no time information (decision D18). In every dataset cleaning removed less than 5 % of the citations.

DatasetPapersCitationsDensityCite nothingNever citedMax in / outSeparate pieces

Table 7 and Figure 7 show what the networks share: no loops, most papers cited once or never, a few heavily cited ones. They differ in size and connectivity: PubMed-Diabetes is about seven times larger than Cora and is one connected piece, Cora has 78 and CiteSeer 390 separate pieces. In the two smaller networks far fewer papers cite nothing.

7. Do the results hold on Cora and CiteSeer?

Table 8. How well the forests predict PageRank on held-out papers in each dataset. The last column is the best single centrality on its own (Spearman with PageRank).
DatasetR² with PageRank (control)R² without (primary)Spearman primaryBest single centrality

The two forests (Table 8, Figure 8). The control copies its PageRank input in all three datasets (99.5 % or more of its weight), so the reason for the primary forest does not depend on the dataset. In Cora and CiteSeer closeness alone already follows PageRank closely, and the primary forest is mostly a copy of closeness.

Stability (Figure 9, Figure 10, Figure 11). The advantage over PageRank at the top of the ranking is found only in PubMed-Diabetes. In Cora and CiteSeer the primary forest is not more stable than PageRank: the average differences are -0.010 and -0.003 in Spearman and -0.06 and -0.04 in top-10 % stay, and it beats PageRank at the top in 0 of 9 settings in both. As in PubMed-Diabetes, it is never more stable than the best single measure (Table 9).

8. Does the forest do better without closeness?

Why we tested it. Closeness is the one feature whose Phase A formula had to be changed (decision D17), and it is the feature the primary forest relies on most. The test removes closeness completely: from the features, from both forests and from the list of single measures; nothing else changes. The test has its own settings and result folders; the main code still computes closeness.

Table 10. What removing closeness changes for the primary forest. The change columns are averages over the 9 damage settings (negative = less stable without closeness). The last column counts the settings in which the forest keeps the top 10 % more stable than PageRank, with and without closeness.
DatasetCloseness weight in the forestHold-out R²Change in SpearmanChange in top-10 % staySettings better than PageRank
PubMed-Diabetes47 %0.75 to 0.26+0.028-0.0366 to 6 of 9
Cora90 %0.67 to 0.28-0.105-0.0580 to 0 of 9
CiteSeer94 %0.84 to 0.45-0.082-0.0260 to 0 of 9

Accuracy. In all three datasets the forest predicts PageRank clearly worse without closeness (Figure 12): R² falls by 0.49 in PubMed-Diabetes, 0.39 in Cora and 0.38 in CiteSeer.

Stability (Table 10, Figure 13). The effect differs between datasets. In Cora and CiteSeer the forest is less stable without closeness (-0.105 and -0.082 in Spearman). In PubMed-Diabetes the order over all papers is slightly more stable (+0.028) but the top 10 % is less stable (-0.036); this small gain comes with a forest that predicts PageRank far worse (R² 0.26) and leans on degree and k-core.

Answer to the lecturer's two questions
  • Better results without closeness? No for accuracy (all three datasets). For stability it depends on the dataset: worse in Cora and CiteSeer, mixed in PubMed-Diabetes. We recommend keeping closeness.
  • The same on other citation networks? Partly. The reason for the primary forest and the loss of accuracy without closeness are the same in all three; the advantage over PageRank at the top of the ranking, and the effect of closeness on stability, are not.

10. Limits of these results

  • Three datasets, all small to medium citation graphs of scientific papers. Their differences show that one dataset is not enough for a general claim.
  • One target. The forests learn PageRank. Agreeing with PageRank is not the same as measuring true importance, and a ranking can be stable and still wrong.
  • No dates. Citation loops in Cora and CiteSeer were removed with the fewest edges, which is a choice (decision D18).
  • Forest settings. Every tree sees all features at every split (no feature randomness), unlike the usual Random Forest and unlike the argument of Phase A hypothesis H2.
  • Trees cannot extrapolate. After citations are added many scaled inputs leave the range seen in training, and the forest gives those papers the same score. Part of its stability is this effect.
  • Training and testing on the same graph, as in Phase A; the hold-out check only shows that the forest learned something.

Data sources

  • Namata, London, Getoor and Huang (2012), Query-driven active surveying for collective classification, Workshop on Mining and Learning with Graphs (MLG).
  • McCallum, Nigam, Rennie and Seymore (2000), Automating the construction of internet portals with machine learning, Information Retrieval 3(2).
  • Giles, Bollacker and Lawrence (1998), CiteSeer: an automatic citation indexing system, ACM Digital Libraries.
  • Sen, Namata, Bilgic, Getoor, Gallagher and Eliassi-Rad (2008), Collective classification in network data, AI Magazine 29(3).
  • Files: linqs-data.soe.ucsc.edu/public/lbc/ (Cora, CiteSeer) and the PubMed-Diabetes files given for the project.

Reproducing this report

CITATION_DATASET=cora FEATURE_SET=full          python scripts/run_pipeline.py   # about 1 minute
CITATION_DATASET=cora FEATURE_SET=no_closeness  python scripts/run_pipeline.py
(the same for citeseer and pubmed; PubMed with all features can also be built with notebooks 01-08)
python scripts/build_report.py                  # writes results/report/
